claims.claim: H2O2-induced oxidative stress resulted in significant transcript shortening, similar to that observed with arsenite.
claims.source: To exclude potential confounding effects of arsenite itself, we further tested oxidative stress induction with 0.3 mM hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) for 2 hr followed by TERA-seq. H2O2-induced oxidative stress also resulted in significant transcript shortening (Mann–Whitney: p-value<10–96), similar to that observed with arsenite, indicating that oxidative stress results in RNA shortening irrespective of inducer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Oxidative stress results in RNA shortening irrespective of inducer.
claims.source: H2O2-induced oxidative stress also resulted in significant transcript shortening (Mann–Whitney: p-value<10–96), similar to that observed with arsenite, indicating that oxidative stress results in RNA shortening irrespective of inducer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing arsenite and H2O2 treatments.

claims.claim: Heat-shocked K562 cells had significantly shorter RNAs compared to unstressed cells.
claims.source: To explore whether RNA shortening is unique to oxidative stress, we re-examined publicly available direct RNA-seq data for human K562 cells that were subjected to heat shock at 42°C for 60 min (Maier et al., 2020). Our results showed that heat-shocked cells also had significantly shorter RNAs compared to unstressed cells (Mann–Whitney: p-value<10–76), again independently of differential expression (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1i and j).
claims.evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of publicly available data.

claims.claim: RNA shortening was observed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts 3T3 cells treated with sodium arsenite, suggesting an evolutionary conserved process.
claims.source: Additionally, we also observed RNA shortening in mouse embryonic fibroblasts 3T3 cells treated with sodium arsenite, suggesting an evolutionary conserved process (Figure 1—figure supplement 1k and l).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: NanopLen is a tool that uses linear mixed models to identify transcripts with statistically significant RNA length changes.
claims.source: To identify transcripts with statistically significant RNA length changes, we developed NanopLen, a tool that uses linear mixed models, and modeled the library as a random effect to adjust for variation across replicates.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the computational tool developed in the study.

claims.claim: The NanopLen model accurately predicted the true length difference for each tested shortening proportion and had a well-controlled false-positive rate on simulated data.
claims.source: To test the model, we simulated sequencing data over varying RNA shortening proportions and expression counts. The simulated data showed that the model accurately predicted the true length difference for each tested shortening proportion and had a well-controlled false-positive rate (Figure 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: NanopLen identified 2730 significantly shortened transcripts (p-value<0.05) when comparing unstressed and arsenite-treated cells.
claims.source: We subsequently employed NanopLen to compare unstressed and arsenite-treated cells and identified 2730 significantly shortened transcripts (p-value<0.05) (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the NanopLen analysis.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis of the most highly shortened transcripts showed processes relevant to RNA catabolism, translation initiation, and protein localization to the endoplasmic reticulum.
claims.source: Gene ontology analysis of these most highly shortened transcripts showed processes relevant to RNA catabolism, translation initiation, and protein localization to the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Significantly shortened transcripts showed that their 3ʹ templated end was almost identical in oxidative stress and unstressed conditions, whereas the corresponding 5ʹ end was heterogeneous.
claims.source: The presence of a poly(A) tail is required for direct RNA-seq. Therefore, we anticipated that our method would only be able to capture fragmentation occurring at the 5ʹ end of RNAs. As expected, significantly shortened transcripts showed that their 3ʹ templated end was almost identical in oxidative stress and unstressed conditions, whereas the corresponding 5ʹ end was heterogeneous (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Transcriptome-wide quantification confirmed that the 3ʹ end was almost identical in oxidative stress and unstressed conditions, whereas the 5ʹ end was heterogeneous.
claims.source: Quantification at the transcriptome-wide level further confirmed this observation (Mann–Whitney p-value<10–256, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR analysis showed that arsenite-treated cells had substantially reduced amplification from primer pairs closer to the 5ʹ end of the transcript than near the 3ʹ end compared to control cells.
claims.source: To validate our sequencing results, we performed RT-qPCR analysis using pairs of primers targeting regions along each transcript. We found that arsenite-treated cells had substantially reduced amplification from primer pairs closer to the 5ʹ end of the transcript than near the 3ʹ end compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: All stress conditions (heat shock, H2O2, NaAsO2) resulted in significantly reduced read coverage at the 5ʹ end in short-read RNA-seq data from HEK293 cells.
claims.source: We reasoned that RNA shortening at the 5ʹ end should also be reflected in short-read RNA-seq as reduction in read coverage at the 5ʹ end of RNAs. We thus reanalyzed data from HEK293 cells treated with a battery of stressors, that is, 42°C heat shock for 1 hr; 0.6 mM H2O2 for 2 hr; and 300  µM NaAsO2 for 2 hr followed by short-read RNA-seq (Watkins et al., 2022). Our analysis showed that, compared to unstressed, all stress conditions resulted in significantly reduced read coverage at the 5ʹ end (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by reanalysis of publicly available short-read RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Transcription start sites (TSSs) showed nonsignificant changes between stress and unstressed conditions.
claims.source: Finally, we considered the possibility that selection of alternative transcription start sites (TSSs) downstream of annotated TSSs could be contributing to RNA shortening. We have previously established that positions with high read density upstream of coding sequences in TERA-seq accurately represent TSSs matching those defined by CAGE-seq (Ibrahim et al., 2021). We used this method to independently calculate TSSs in stress and unstressed conditions in our HeLa data. Our results showed nonsignificant changes between conditions (Mann–Whitney: p-value=0.35) with no preference toward shorter or longer transcripts (Figure 2f), indicating that the observed shortening is not affected by TSS selection.
claims.evidence: This is supported by TSS analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The observed shortening is not affected by TSS selection.
claims.source: Our results showed nonsignificant changes between conditions (Mann–Whitney: p-value=0.35) with no preference toward shorter or longer transcripts (Figure 2f), indicating that the observed shortening is not affected by TSS selection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on TSS analysis.

claims.claim: The results provide strong evidence for stress-induced decay occurring at the 5ʹ end of RNA molecules harboring poly(A) tails.
claims.source: Collectively, our results, although not excluding 3ʹ end decay for molecules not sequenced due to lack of a poly(A) tail, provide strong evidence for stress-induced decay occurring at the 5ʹ end of RNA molecules harboring poly(A) tails.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: XRN1 is the primary 5ʹ to 3ʹ exonuclease in cells.
claims.source: XRN1 is the primary 5ʹ to 3ʹ exonuclease in cells, and thus a likely candidate for mediating 5ʹ transcript shortening upon stress following decapping or endonucleolytic fragmentation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claims.claim: Silencing of XRN1 with siRNAs resulted in substantial reduction of protein level compared to non-targeted control.
claims.source: Silencing of XRN1 with siRNAs (siXRN1) resulted in substantial reduction of protein level compared to non-targeted control (siCTRL) (Figure 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Silencing of XRN1 largely abolished the transcript length difference between arsenite and unstressed cells.
claims.source: We subsequently performed TERA-seq for siCTRL- and siXRN1-transfected cells in the presence or absence of oxidative stress. Our results showed that while arsenite and unstressed siCTRL cells had the highest transcript length difference (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–307), silencing of XRN1 largely abolished this difference (Mann–Whitney, p-value=0.18) and brought transcript lengths in line with unstressed cells with XRN1 silenced (Figure 3b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: XRN1 silencing showed an even stronger effect on adapter-ligated transcripts, suggesting that stress-induced decay depends on XRN1.
claims.source: Similar results were observed for adapter-ligated transcripts, with XRN1 silencing showing an even stronger effect, suggesting that stress-induced decay depends on XRN1 (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: RNA length rescue upon XRN1 silencing was predominant and specific for the previously identified stress-induced significantly shortened RNAs.
claims.source: While silencing of XRN1 might be expected to have a general effect on RNA length, our results showed that RNA length rescue was predominant and specific for the previously identified stress-induced significantly shortened RNAs identified by our NanopLen analysis (Figure 3d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Under traditional decay models, deadenylation is considered the first and rate-limiting step prior to decapping and subsequent exonucleolytic action from the 5ʹ-end via XRN1.
claims.source: Under traditional decay models, deadenylation is considered the first and rate-limiting step prior to decapping and subsequent exonucleolytic action from the 5ʹ-end via XRN1 (Borbolis and Syntichaki, 2022; Łabno et al., 2016; Mugridge et al., 2018; Passmore and Coller, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge and citations.

claims.claim: The RNA molecules that were found shortened still had a poly(A) tail, arguing that removal of the poly(A) tail was not necessary for stress-induced 5ʹ end shortening.
claims.source: However, the RNA molecules we sequenced and found shortened still had a poly(A) tail, as this is required for dRNA-seq. This argued that removal of the poly(A) tail was not necessary for stress-induced 5ʹ end shortening.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the requirement of poly(A) tails for direct RNA-seq.

claims.claim: Expression of the dominant negative NOT8* form resulted in an expected increase in poly(A) tail length compared to control GFP cells.
claims.source: Expression of the dominant negative NOT8* form was confirmed by epifluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b) and resulted in an expected increase in poly(A) tail length compared to control GFP cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Significant 5ʹ shortening upon stress was observed following expression of the dominant negative NOT8*, suggesting that deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex was not required for stress-induced 5ʹ RNA decay.
claims.source: As hypothesized, our results identified significant 5ʹ shortening upon stress following expression of the dominant negative NOT8* (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–299), suggesting that deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex was indeed not required for stress-induced 5ʹ RNA decay (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Transcripts from DCP2*-expressing cells presented a similar significant 5ʹ shortening upon oxidative stress as GFP control cells, suggesting that the canonical decapping pathway is not necessary for stress-induced RNA decay.
claims.source: Interestingly, transcripts from DCP2*-expressing cells presented a similar significant (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–127) 5ʹ shortening upon oxidative stress as GFP control cells, suggesting that the canonical decapping pathway is also not necessary for stress-induced RNA decay, and thus likely involves an endonucleolytic cleavage event (Figure 3f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Stress-induced RNA decay likely involves an endonucleolytic cleavage event.
claims.source: Interestingly, transcripts from DCP2*-expressing cells presented a similar significant (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–127) 5ʹ shortening upon oxidative stress as GFP control cells, suggesting that the canonical decapping pathway is also not necessary for stress-induced RNA decay, and thus likely involves an endonucleolytic cleavage event (Figure 3f).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the independence from decapping.

claims.claim: Stress-induced RNA decay is mediated by XRN1 but is independent of prior deadenylation or decapping.
claims.source: In conclusion, our results show that stress-induced RNA decay is mediated by XRN1 but is independent of prior deadenylation or decapping.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: The yeast Xrn1 has previously been associated with the decay of oxidized RNAs via the No-Go decay pathway following ribosome stalling at nucleotide adducts, particularly 8-OxoG, and endonucleolytic cleavage.
claims.source: The yeast Xrn1 has previously been associated with the decay of oxidized RNAs via the No-Go decay pathway following ribosome stalling at nucleotide adducts, particularly 8-OxoG, and endonucleolytic cleavage (Yan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: No G-nucleotide enrichment difference between arsenite and unstressed conditions was observed at the vicinity of 5ʹ ends of sequenced RNAs.
claims.source: We reasoned that if endonucleolytic cleavage induced by 8-OxoG was the major contributor to transcript shortening during oxidative stress, then an increase in guanine prevalence should be expected at the vicinity of 5ʹ ends of sequenced RNAs upon stress. However, our data did not support this explanation as no G-nucleotide enrichment difference between arsenite and unstressed conditions was observed (Figure 4a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by nucleotide composition analysis shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The stress-induced RNA decay described is not mediated via 8-OxoG ribosome stalling.
claims.source: These findings, combined with the presence of shortening under heat shock (Figure 1h), indicate that the stress-induced RNA decay described here is not mediated via 8-OxoG ribosome stalling.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of G-nucleotide enrichment and heat shock data.

claims.claim: Annotated length, coding sequence length, and GC content were significantly associated with stress-induced 5ʹ shortening.
claims.source: To identify gene features that could be driving stress-induced RNA decay, we tested whether the annotated nucleotide content and transcript length were predictive of transcripts prone to stress-induced 5ʹ shortening. Our results showed a significant association with the annotated length, coding sequence length, and GC content, both being significantly lower for significantly shortened transcripts (Figure 4b–d) and only a minor association with the 5ʹ and 3ʹ UTR length (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Pre-stress ribosome density per RNA was not associated with stress-induced shortening.
claims.source: Since the coding sequence is the primary region of ribosome occupancy, we tested whether pre-stress ribosome density could be defining 5ʹ shortening using publicly available ribosome profiling data from unstressed cells (Park et al., 2016). Our analysis found no association between ribosome density per RNA and stress-induced shortening (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e), indicating that the pre-stress ribosome levels on RNAs are not linked to RNA decay under stress.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Pre-stress ribosome levels on RNAs are not linked to RNA decay under stress.
claims.source: Our analysis found no association between ribosome density per RNA and stress-induced shortening (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d and e), indicating that the pre-stress ribosome levels on RNAs are not linked to RNA decay under stress.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on ribosome profiling analysis.

claims.claim: ISRIB bypasses the effect of eIF2α phosphorylation and facilitates translation initiation under stress.
claims.source: To test the role of translation initiation inhibition and ribosome run-off upon stress on stress-induced decay, we treated cells with the ISR inhibitor (ISRIB) that bypasses the effect of eIF2α phosphorylation and facilitates translation initiation under stress (Rabouw et al., 2019; Sidrauski et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on citations to previous research.

claims.claim: ISRIB had no noticeable effect on the dose-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α but inhibited the SG formation under stress.
claims.source: We confirmed that ISRIB had no noticeable effect on the dose-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α but inhibited the SG formation under stress, as expected (Figure 5a–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Polysome fractionation following ISRIB addition showed a clear reduction of the monosome fraction, indicating partial recovery of translation initiation.
claims.source: Polysome fractionation following ISRIB addition showed a clear reduction of the monosome fraction, indicating partial recovery of translation initiation, as previously described (Sidrauski et al., 2013; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in the figure and citations.

claims.claim: ISRIB treatment resulted in a significant shift of RNA length toward longer molecules, essentially restoring transcript length to the level observed in unstressed cells.
claims.source: We then performed TERA-Seq on ISRIB-treated and control cells in the presence or absence of arsenite. Our results showed that compared to cells treated with arsenite only, ISRIB treatment resulted in a significant shift of RNA length toward longer molecules (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–156) essentially restoring transcript length to the level observed in unstressed cells (Figure 5e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Previously identified significantly shortened transcripts showed the greatest recovery of their length upon ISRIB treatment compared to nonsignificant ones.
claims.source: Importantly, previously identified significantly shortened transcripts showed the greatest recovery of their length compared to nonsignificant ones (Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The observed shift in length upon ISRIB treatment is independent of differential expression status.
claims.source: To test whether this could be simply attributed to a possible length imbalance between up- and downregulated genes, we again plotted the average transcript length stratified by the differential expression status. Our data show that the observed shift in length is independent of differential expression status (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a and b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Stress-induced RNA decay is associated with RNAs leaving the translation pool following translation initiation inhibition upon stress.
claims.source: These results indicated that stress-induced RNA decay is associated with RNAs, leaving the translation pool following translation initiation inhibition upon stress.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on ISRIB treatment results.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide blocks elongation and traps ribosomes on RNAs along with translation factors in polysomes, thus decreasing SG formation.
claims.source: As an alternative to ISRIB which modulates translation initiation, we also treated cells with cycloheximide to interrogate the dynamics of ribosome elongation and to prevent ribosome run-off. Cycloheximide blocks elongation and thus traps ribosomes on RNAs along with translation factors in polysomes, thus decreasing SG formation (Jayabalan et al., 2021; Kedersha and Anderson, 2007; Takahashi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Treatment with cycloheximide reduced the monosome fraction, although to a lower degree than ISRIB.
claims.source: We confirmed that treatment with cycloheximide also reduced the monosome fraction, although to a lower degree than ISRIB (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Cycloheximide treatment inhibited RNA decay, particularly for the most significantly shortened RNAs, largely rescuing their length.
claims.source: Interestingly, cycloheximide treatment also inhibited RNA decay, particularly for the most significantly shortened RNAs largely rescuing their length (Figure 5g–i).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Translation initiation inhibition and the exit of mRNAs from the translational pool is a critical step towards stress-induced decay.
claims.source: Combined, our results indicate translation initiation inhibition and the exit of mRNAs from the translational pool as a critical step towards stress-induced decay.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on ISRIB and cycloheximide treatment results.

claims.claim: SG-enriched genes were generally significantly longer, particularly in their coding and 3ʹ UTR sequences, and less expressed than SG-depleted ones.
claims.source: To test whether transcripts subject to stress-induced decay associate with SGs, we used publicly available data representing genes enriched in the SG transcriptome (Khong et al., 2017). As previously described (Khong et al., 2017), we found that SG-enriched genes were generally significantly longer, particularly in their coding and 3ʹ UTR sequences, (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) and less expressed than SG-depleted ones (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available data and shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SG-enriched genes were shortened at a significantly higher level upon oxidative stress than SG-depleted or nonlocalized RNAs for both HeLa and U-2 OS cells.
claims.source: However, differential gene length analysis showed a significant difference in gene shortening dependent on SG enrichment status. Specifically, SG-enriched genes were found to be shortened at a significantly higher level upon oxidative stress than SG-depleted or nonlocalized RNAs for both HeLa and U-2 OS cells (Figure 6b and c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential length analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: SG-enriched RNAs harbored lower GC content, similar to significantly shortened transcripts.
claims.source: Consistent with stress-induced gene shortening being associated with SG enrichment, SG-enriched RNAs harbored lower GC content (Figure 6d), similar to significantly shortened transcripts (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GC content analysis shown in the figures.

claims.claim: No association was found between P-body localization and gene lengths.
claims.source: To test whether the observed enrichment of shortened genes is specific to the SGs, we also tested for association with processing bodies (P-bodies), membrane-less organelles enriched in de-capping factors and exoribonucleases that are essential for RNA decay under normal, nonstress conditions (Brothers et al., 2023). We reanalyzed previously published data from HEK293 cells (Matheny et al., 2019), but in contrast to SGs, we found no association between P-body localization and gene lengths (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of publicly available data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: No association was found between P-body localization and RNA shortening.
claims.source: We also did not find an association between P-body localization and RNA shortening, which however could be a result of comparing different cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in the figure, with a caveat about cell line differences.

claims.claim: Shortened RNAs exhibit similar properties to SG-enriched transcripts and are preferentially enriched in the SG transcriptome.
claims.source: Our data show that shortened RNAs exhibit similar properties to SG-enriched transcripts and are preferentially enriched in the SG transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple analyses of SG-enriched transcripts.

claims.claim: ΔΔG3BP1/2 U-2 OS cells inhibit SG condensation in response to arsenite and other stressors.
claims.source: To test the role of SGs in stress-induced RNA decay, we employed control (WT) U-2 OS and U-2 OS cells genetically ablated for both G3BP1 and G3BP2 (ΔΔG3BP1/2) via CRISPR/Cas9 (gift from Paul Anderson lab) previously developed and characterized in Kedersha et al., 2016. ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells inhibit SG condensation in response to arsenite and other stressors.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the cell line used, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Treatment of WT U-2 OS cells with arsenite showed a highly significant and global shortening of RNA upon stress.
claims.source: Treatment of WT U-2 OS cells with arsenite showed a highly significant and global shortening of RNA upon stress (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–307) in stark contrast to ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells that showed substantially less shortening (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–5) (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1g and h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells showed substantially less shortening upon arsenite treatment compared to WT cells.
claims.source: Treatment of WT U-2 OS cells with arsenite showed a highly significant and global shortening of RNA upon stress (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–307) in stark contrast to ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells that showed substantially less shortening (Mann–Whitney, p-value<10–5) (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1g and h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Inhibition of G3BP1/2-mediated SG formation rescued RNA length to the level of unstressed WT cells.
claims.source: Further comparison of ΔΔG3BP1/2 and WT U-2 OS showed that inhibition of G3BP1/2-mediated SG formation rescued RNA length to the level of unstressed WT cells (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 1i and j).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TERA-seq data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: G3BP1/2-mediated SG formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay.
claims.source: These results indicate that G3BP1/2-mediated SG formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ΔΔG3BP1/2 cell experiments.

claims.claim: A comparison of differentially expressed transcripts upon arsenite treatment in ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells showed no association with WT shortening, indicating that in the absence of SGs these RNAs are not rapidly eliminated.
claims.source: Alternatively, SGs could be protective of shortened RNAs that otherwise would be rapidly eliminated from cells. Under this assumption, stress-shortened RNAs identified in WT cells would be expected to be depleted in ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells during stress. A comparison of differentially expressed transcripts upon arsenite treatment in ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells showed no association with WT shortening, indicating that in the absence of SGs these RNAs are not rapidly eliminated (Figure 6g), consistent with previous findings (Bley et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in the figure and a citation.

claims.claim: G3BP1/2-dependent SG formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay.
claims.source: Collectively our results show that G3BP1/2-dependent SG formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experiments with ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells.

claims.claim: TERA-seq involves the ligation of unique adapters at the 5ʹ end of RNAs to address a key limitation in nanopore direct RNA sequencing – the inability to consistently capture the 5ʹ end of sequenced RNA molecules.
claims.source: In this work, we used TERA-seq, a protocol that involves the ligation of unique adapters at the 5ʹ end of RNAs (Ibrahim et al., 2021) to address a key limitation in nanopore direct RNA sequencing – the inability to consistently capture the 5ʹ end of sequenced RNA molecules.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Stress triggers decay at the 5′ end of RNAs.
claims.source: By sequencing RNA molecules end-to-end, we show that stress triggers decay at the 5′ end of RNAs.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: Stress-induced 5ʹ end decay leaves 'scars' that can be identified in traditional short-read RNA-seq as decreased read density at the 5ʹ end of transcripts.
claims.source: Interestingly our results show that stress-induced 5ʹ end decay leaves 'scars' that can also be identified in traditional short-read RNA-seq as decreased read density at the 5ʹ end of transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is a finding based on reanalysis of short-read RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: XRN1 is an essential component for stress-induced decay, in the absence of which the RNA length is largely rescued.
claims.source: Our findings highlight XRN1 as an essential component for stress-induced decay, in the absence of which the RNA length is largely rescued.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on XRN1 knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The data point towards endonucleolytic cleavage as the most likely mechanism for the initial cut on RNA, generating either a 5ʹP directly recognized by XRN1 or a 5ʹOH that is subsequently phosphorylated to become a substrate for XRN1.
claims.source: Instead, our data point towards endonucleolytic cleavage as the most likely mechanism for the initial cut on RNA, generating either a 5ʹP directly recognized by XRN1 or a 5ʹOH that is subsequently phosphorylated to become a substrate for XRN1 (Navickas et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the independence from deadenylation and decapping, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Transcript shortening is suppressed by treatments that increase ribosome occupancy (ISRIB and cycloheximide), suggesting that the putative endonucleolytic cut is likely not due to No-Go decay or a related ribosome quality control pathway.
claims.source: Our analysis showing that transcript shortening is suppressed by treatments that increase ribosome occupancy (ISRIB and cycloheximide) also suggests that this putative endonucleolytic cut is likely not due to No-Go decay or a related ribosome quality control pathway since these decay mechanisms are guided to cleavage sites by ribosome collisions (Doma and Parker, 2006).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ISRIB and cycloheximide treatment results and a citation.

claims.claim: It is currently unknown whether a mechanistic link exists with other co-translational decay pathways, such as ribothrypsis.
claims.source: However, it is currently unknown whether a mechanistic link exists with other co-translational decay pathways, such as ribothrypsis (Ibrahim et al., 2018), that also initiate by endonucleolysis.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Recent studies have found sporadic fragments of 3' UTRs as products of No-Go decay occurring at the sites of translation termination in oxidative stress, development, and brain aging.
claims.source: Recent studies have found sporadic fragments of 3' UTRs as products of No-Go decay occurring at the sites of translation termination in oxidative stress, development, and brain aging (Ji et al., 2021; Sudmant et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: It is possible that some shorter fragments could be contributing to an accumulation of 3' UTRs under stress conditions.
claims.source: While most stress-induced decay fragments are longer than 3' UTRs and are not confined to translation termination sites, it is possible that some shorter fragments could also be contributing to an accumulation of 3' UTRs under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible contribution.

claims.claim: Short coding sequences and low GC content were found as features of transcripts that are subject to stress-induced decay.
claims.source: Short coding sequences and low GC content were found as features of transcripts that are subject to stress-induced decay, arguing that there may be a component of structural stability to the specificity of 5' end shortening.
claims.evidence: This is a finding based on correlation analysis.

claims.claim: There may be a component of structural stability to the specificity of 5' end shortening.
claims.source: Short coding sequences and low GC content were found as features of transcripts that are subject to stress-induced decay, arguing that there may be a component of structural stability to the specificity of 5' end shortening.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the association with GC content.

claims.claim: Low GC content appears to be a determinant for RNA recruitment to SGs.

results.result: Cellular stress induces widespread 5' end RNA decay. RNAs from oxidatively stressed cells (arsenite, H2O2) and heat-shocked cells were significantly shorter than unstressed cells by an average of 115.3 nucleotides. This shortening was independent of differential expression, coding potential, and transcription start site selection, and was validated by RT-qPCR and short-read RNA-seq analysis showing reduced 5' end coverage.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C50 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (direct RNA-seq, meta-length analysis, adapter-ligated reads, RT-qPCR, short-read RNA-seq reanalysis, TSS analysis) across different stress conditions (arsenite, H2O2, heat shock) and cell types (HeLa, K562, mouse 3T3). The statistical significance is strong (p-values < 10^-76 to 10^-307), and multiple controls exclude technical artifacts and alternative explanations.

results.result: Development and validation of NanopLen statistical framework. The authors developed NanopLen, a linear mixed model-based tool to identify transcripts with statistically significant RNA length changes. Simulation testing showed accurate prediction of length differences with well-controlled false-positive rates. Application to arsenite-treated cells identified 2730 significantly shortened transcripts enriched for RNA catabolism, translation initiation, and ER protein localization processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 describe a new computational method with appropriate validation through simulation (C41) and biological application (C42-C43). The simulation results demonstrate the method's accuracy and statistical control, and the biological findings show expected enrichment patterns consistent with stress response.

results.result: Stress-induced RNA decay is XRN1-dependent. siRNA-mediated silencing of XRN1 largely abolished the transcript length difference between arsenite-treated and unstressed cells (p-value changed from <10^-307 to 0.18). The rescue effect was even stronger for adapter-ligated transcripts and was specific to previously identified significantly shortened RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 provide strong evidence through knockdown experiments with appropriate controls. The dramatic change in statistical significance (from p<10^-307 to p=0.18) and specificity for shortened transcripts (C55) support the conclusion. However, the knockdown is not complete (substantial but not total protein reduction shown in C52), which could affect interpretation.

results.result: Stress-induced RNA decay is independent of deadenylation and decapping. Expression of dominant-negative NOT8* (blocking deadenylation) or DCP2* (blocking decapping) did not prevent 5' RNA shortening upon stress (p-values <10^-299 and <10^-127 respectively). Since shortened RNAs retained poly(A) tails and decay occurred without deadenylation or decapping, the mechanism likely involves endonucleolytic cleavage followed by XRN1-mediated degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 challenge the canonical decay model through dominant-negative experiments. The poly(A) tail retention (C57) is a logical inference from the sequencing method requirement. The NOT8* experiment shows clear poly(A) tail lengthening (C58) confirming its function, yet shortening still occurs (C59). The DCP2* result (C60) is noted to have weaker expression than NOT8*, which could affect interpretation. The endonucleolytic cleavage conclusion (C61, C97) is a reasonable inference but remains indirect.

results.result: Stress-induced RNA decay is not mediated by 8-OxoG ribosome stalling. No G-nucleotide enrichment was observed at the vicinity of 5' ends of sequenced RNAs in arsenite-treated versus unstressed conditions. Combined with the observation of shortening under heat shock (which does not produce 8-OxoG), this indicates the mechanism differs from previously described oxidized RNA decay via No-Go decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 appropriately test and exclude a specific mechanistic hypothesis. The nucleotide composition analysis (C64) directly addresses the 8-OxoG hypothesis, and the heat shock data (C65) provides orthogonal evidence. The logic is sound and the conclusion is appropriately limited to excluding this specific mechanism.

results.result: Transcript features associated with stress-induced decay. Significantly shortened transcripts had shorter annotated length, shorter coding sequences, and lower GC content. Pre-stress ribosome density per RNA was not associated with stress-induced shortening, indicating that pre-stress ribosome levels are not linked to RNA decay under stress. These features suggest a component of structural stability in the specificity of 5' end shortening.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 present correlation analyses with appropriate statistical testing. The lack of association with pre-stress ribosome density (C67-C68) is important for excluding certain mechanistic models. However, these are correlative observations that do not establish causation. The inference about structural stability (C103) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Translation initiation inhibition and ribosome run-off are critical for stress-induced decay. ISRIB treatment, which bypasses eIF2α phosphorylation and facilitates translation initiation, restored RNA length to unstressed levels (p<10^-156) without affecting eIF2α phosphorylation. The effect was strongest for previously identified shortened transcripts and independent of differential expression. This indicates that stress-induced RNA decay is associated with RNAs leaving the translation pool following translation initiation inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 provide strong evidence through pharmacological intervention with appropriate controls. The ISRIB mechanism is well-established (C69), its effects are validated by polysome profiling (C71), and the specificity for shortened transcripts (C73) strengthens the conclusion. The independence from differential expression (C74) excludes a simple transcriptional explanation. However, ISRIB also inhibits SG formation (C70), which confounds interpretation of whether the effect is due to translation reinitiation or SG dissolution.

results.result: Cycloheximide treatment inhibits stress-induced RNA decay. Cycloheximide, which blocks elongation and traps ribosomes on RNAs, also inhibited RNA decay and largely rescued the length of significantly shortened RNAs. This provides additional evidence that ribosome occupancy protects against stress-induced decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide complementary evidence to the ISRIB experiments using a different mechanism (elongation block vs. initiation facilitation). The cycloheximide effect was weaker than ISRIB in reducing monosome fraction (C77), yet still showed rescue of RNA length (C78), supporting the interpretation. However, like ISRIB, cycloheximide also affects SG formation, creating similar confounding issues.

results.result: The endonucleolytic cleavage mechanism is likely not No-Go decay. Transcript shortening is suppressed by treatments that increase ribosome occupancy (ISRIB and cycloheximide), suggesting the putative endonucleolytic cut is not due to No-Go decay or related ribosome quality control pathways, since these mechanisms are guided to cleavage sites by ribosome collisions.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 presents a logical inference based on the ISRIB and cycloheximide results. The reasoning is sound: if ribosome collisions were driving cleavage, increasing ribosome occupancy should increase rather than decrease decay. However, this remains an indirect argument and does not definitively exclude all ribosome quality control pathways.

results.result: Shortened RNAs are enriched in the stress granule transcriptome. SG-enriched genes were significantly more shortened upon oxidative stress than SG-depleted or nonlocalized RNAs in both HeLa and U-2 OS cells. SG-enriched RNAs harbored lower GC content, similar to significantly shortened transcripts, and low GC content appears to be a determinant for RNA recruitment to SGs.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 and C104-C105 establish correlation between SG enrichment and RNA shortening through analysis of published SG transcriptome data. The consistency across cell lines (C81) and the shared GC content feature (C82, C104) strengthen the association. However, these are correlative observations from published data, not direct experimental evidence from the current study.

results.result: No association between P-body localization and RNA shortening. Analysis of published P-body localization data from HEK293 cells found no association between P-body localization and gene lengths or RNA shortening, in contrast to stress granules. However, this could result from comparing different cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 present negative results from analysis of published data. The authors appropriately note the caveat about different cell lines (C84), which significantly limits interpretation. The lack of association could be biological or technical, and the cross-cell-line comparison is a major limitation.

results.result: G3BP1/2-mediated stress granule formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay. ΔΔG3BP1/2 U-2 OS cells, which cannot form stress granules, showed substantially less RNA shortening upon arsenite treatment (p<10^-5) compared to WT cells (p<10^-307). Genetic ablation of G3BP1/2 rescued RNA length to the level of unstressed WT cells, indicating that SG formation is required and indispensable for stress-induced decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 provide the strongest evidence for SG requirement through genetic ablation experiments. The dramatic difference in statistical significance between WT and knockout cells (p<10^-307 vs p<10^-5) is compelling. The rescue to unstressed levels (C89) is particularly strong evidence. The cell line is well-characterized from prior work (C86). However, G3BP1/2 may have functions beyond SG formation, so the effect could be partially independent of SG formation per se.

results.result: Shortened RNAs are not rapidly eliminated in the absence of stress granules. Comparison of differentially expressed transcripts upon arsenite treatment in ΔΔG3BP1/2 cells showed no association with WT shortening, indicating that in the absence of SGs these RNAs are not rapidly eliminated.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 tests an alternative hypothesis (that SGs are protective rather than promoting decay) and appropriately excludes it through differential expression analysis. The lack of association with WT shortening and consistency with prior findings (Bley et al., 2015) support the conclusion. This strengthens the interpretation that SGs promote rather than prevent decay.

results.result: Stress granule formation may promote RNA decay through tethering with P-bodies. The critical role of SG formation in stress-induced RNA decay may occur through tethering with P-bodies, which are dynamically linked with SGs under stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is explicitly speculative ('perhaps through tethering') and supported only by citations to prior work showing SG-P-body interactions. No direct evidence for this mechanism is provided in the current study. This is appropriately presented as a hypothesis for future investigation.

results.result: Background on cellular stress response and RNA metabolism. The manuscript provides context on cellular stress responses, the integrated stress response (ISR), stress granule formation, and prior evidence for both RNA stabilization and decay under stress conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C18 present background information supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the context and knowledge gaps that motivate the study. The claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Experimental design and validation of TERA-seq approach. The study used arsenite treatment to induce oxidative stress in HeLa cells, verified stress response markers (SG formation, eIF2α phosphorylation, cell viability), and performed TERA-seq with biological triplicates yielding ~2 million reads per library. The approach captured expected stress response gene expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C31 describe the experimental design and quality control measures. The stress induction is validated (C20), cell viability is monitored (C21), technical quality is demonstrated (C28), and biological validation through differential expression and gene ontology is shown (C29-C31). These establish that the experimental system is working as expected.

results.result: Speculative discussion of mechanisms and physiological roles. The authors discuss potential mechanistic links to other decay pathways (ribothrypsis, 3' UTR fragments) and hypothesize that stress-induced RNA decay may have evolved to reduce translational load during stress through multiple mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C112 are explicitly speculative or identify knowledge gaps. C99 and C110 acknowledge what is unknown. C101, C111, and C112 present hypotheses without supporting data. These are appropriately presented as discussion points and future directions rather than established findings.

results.result: Main conclusions of the study. The authors conclude that cellular stress induces prevalent 5' end RNA decay coupled to translation and ribosome occupancy, dependent on XRN1 but independent of deadenylation or decapping, with decaying RNAs enriched in stress granules, and that RNA decay is a key component of RNA metabolism upon cellular stress dependent on stress granule formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 represent the main conclusions synthesized from the experimental results. These are well-supported by the collective evidence from multiple experimental approaches (RNA-seq, knockdowns, dominant negatives, pharmacological interventions, genetic ablations). The conclusions are appropriately qualified and acknowledge limitations (e.g., not excluding 3' end decay for non-poly(A) RNAs in C50).

results.result: The authors report that cellular stress (arsenite, H2O2, heat shock) induces global RNA shortening, with RNAs from stressed cells being significantly shorter than unstressed cells by an average of 115.3 nucleotides. This shortening is independent of differential expression, coding potential, and is observed across multiple stress types and cell lines including mouse cells, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved process.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'describes mRNA shortening during cellular stress' using 'convincing data.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'conclude that cellular stress induces prevalent 5' end RNA decay' and calls the findings 'paradigm-shifting.' Reviewer 3 observes 'a population of transcripts that are shortened during stress' and Reviewer 4 confirms the work 'reveals that cellular stress induces prevalent 5' end RNA decay.' No concerns are raised about this core observation.

results.result: The authors developed NanopLen, a statistical tool using linear mixed models to identify transcripts with significant RNA length changes. The model was validated on simulated data and identified 2,730 significantly shortened transcripts in arsenite-treated cells, with gene ontology analysis showing enrichment for RNA catabolism, translation initiation, and protein localization processes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the methodological innovation without critique. Reviewer 1 describes 'cutting-edge technologies' and Reviewer 2 states the authors 'fully established these paradigm-shifting findings using cutting-edge technologies.' Reviewer 4 calls it 'an exciting and novel discovery utilizing innovative sequencing methods.' The statistical framework and its application are accepted as valid.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that stress-induced RNA shortening occurs specifically at the 5' end while the 3' end remains stable. This was validated by multiple approaches: direct sequencing showing heterogeneous 5' ends but identical 3' ends, RT-qPCR showing reduced amplification near 5' ends, reanalysis of short-read RNA-seq showing reduced 5' coverage, and TSS analysis showing no contribution from alternative transcription start sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this directionality finding without question. Reviewer 2 explicitly states the authors 'conclude that cellular stress induces prevalent 5' end RNA decay' and Reviewer 4 confirms 'cellular stress induces prevalent 5' end RNA decay.' The multiple validation approaches are implicitly accepted through the reviewers' overall positive assessment of the data quality.

results.result: The authors show that stress-induced RNA decay is dependent on the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN1, as XRN1 knockdown largely abolished transcript length differences between stressed and unstressed cells. This rescue effect was specific to stress-shortened transcripts identified by NanopLen analysis.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm XRN1 dependence. Reviewer 2 states 'stress-induced RNA decay is dependent on XRN1,' Reviewer 3 notes 'this shortening is mediated by the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN1, as XRN1 knockdown results in longer transcripts,' and Reviewer 4 confirms 'This decay, however, is dependent on XRN1.' No concerns are raised about this conclusion.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that stress-induced RNA decay does not require deadenylation or decapping, contrary to canonical decay models. Expression of dominant-negative NOT8* (blocking deadenylation) or DCP2* (blocking decapping) did not prevent stress-induced 5' shortening, and shortened RNAs retained poly(A) tails. The authors conclude decay likely involves endonucleolytic cleavage.
results.evaluation: All reviewers highlight this as a key paradigm-shifting finding. Reviewer 1 states 'this mRNA shortening does not appear to require the shortening of poly A tails' and calls it 'Surprising.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'Contrary to the literature...stress-induced RNA decay...does not depend on the removal of the poly(A) tail.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Interestingly, the authors do not observe a polyA-tail shortening.' Reviewer 4 confirms decay is 'independent of the shortening of the poly(A) tail.' This independence from canonical pathways is universally accepted.

results.result: The authors show that stress-induced RNA decay is coupled to translation status. Treatment with ISRIB (restoring translation initiation) or cycloheximide (blocking elongation) rescued RNA length, particularly for significantly shortened transcripts. This indicates that translation initiation inhibition and mRNA exit from the translational pool are critical for stress-induced decay.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the coupling to translation. Reviewer 2 states findings show decay is 'coupled to translation and ribosome occupancy,' and Reviewer 4 similarly confirms decay is 'coupled to translation and ribosome occupancy.' The ISRIB and cycloheximide experiments supporting this conclusion are not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that RNAs undergoing stress-induced decay are predominantly enriched in the stress granule transcriptome. SG-enriched genes showed significantly higher shortening upon oxidative stress compared to SG-depleted or non-localized RNAs, and shared features like lower GC content with shortened transcripts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the stress granule enrichment. Reviewer 1 states 'this shortening is dependent on localization in stress granules,' Reviewer 2 notes decay is 'enriched in the stress granule transcriptome,' and Reviewer 4 confirms decay is 'enriched in the stress granule transcriptome.' The association is accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors show that stress granule formation is required for stress-induced RNA decay. Genetic ablation of G3BP1/2, which prevents SG formation, substantially reduced RNA shortening and rescued RNA length to unstressed levels. This demonstrates that G3BP1/2-mediated SG formation is indispensable for the decay process.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this requirement. Reviewer 1 notes 'this shortening is dependent on localization in stress granules,' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors use G3BP1 knockout cells to demonstrate that stress granule formation is required for the observed transcript shortening,' and Reviewer 4 confirms 'inhibiting stress granule formation in G3BP1/2-null cells restores the RNA length...and suppresses stress-induced decay.' The G3BP1/2 knockout data convincingly establish SG dependence in all reviewers' assessments.

results.result: The authors investigated potential mechanisms and found that stress-induced decay is not mediated by 8-OxoG ribosome stalling (no G-nucleotide enrichment at 5' ends). Shortened transcripts were associated with shorter coding sequences and lower GC content, but pre-stress ribosome density was not predictive of shortening.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these mechanistic findings. The negative results (no 8-OxoG mechanism, no pre-stress ribosome association) and positive associations (CDS length, GC content) are implicitly accepted as part of the overall 'convincing data' (Reviewer 1) and 'paradigm-shifting findings' (Reviewer 2) without specific critique.

results.result: The authors established their experimental system by treating HeLa cells with arsenite to induce oxidative stress, verifying stress granule formation and eIF2α phosphorylation, confirming cell viability, and performing TERA-seq with high-quality replicates showing expected stress response gene expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the experimental setup without concern. The quality control measures and validation of stress induction are implicitly endorsed through reviewers' statements about 'convincing data' (Reviewer 1) and proper use of 'cutting-edge technologies' (Reviewer 2). No methodological concerns are raised about the basic experimental design.

results.result: The authors employed TERA-seq, a nanopore-based direct RNA sequencing method with 5' adapter ligation, to address the limitation of inconsistent 5' end capture in standard direct RNA-seq. This approach allows full-length sequencing of RNA molecules and identification of 5' ends.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the methodological approach. Reviewer 1 describes 'cutting-edge technologies,' Reviewer 2 notes the use of 'direct RNA sequencing with nanopores, enhanced by 5' end adaptor ligation,' and Reviewer 4 highlights 'direct RNA sequencing with a Nanopore-based method' as enabling the discoveries. The technical approach is viewed as a strength.

results.result: The authors conclude that RNA decay is a key component of RNA metabolism during cellular stress that depends on stress granule formation. They propose endonucleolytic cleavage as the initiating mechanism (not No-Go decay), potentially involving SG-P-body interactions, though mechanistic details remain to be fully elucidated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the main conclusion while recognizing it as a significant advance. Reviewer 1 calls the findings 'novel, paradigm-shifting,' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'fully established these paradigm-shifting findings,' Reviewer 3 notes the manuscript 'contains intriguing findings,' and Reviewer 4 calls it 'an exciting and novel discovery.' The proposed model is accepted as well-supported by the data, even if mechanistic details remain incomplete.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological innovation (C40-C43). Both evaluations support the new computational method and its validation. OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of simulation and biological application, while peer reviewers praise it as 'cutting-edge' and 'innovative sequencing methods' without specific critique.

Strong agreement on stress granule requirement (C86-C92, C106). Both evaluations fully support the G3BP1/2 knockout findings. OpenEval notes the dramatic statistical change (p<10^-307 to p<10^-5) and acknowledges G3BP1/2 may have SG-independent functions. Peer reviewers unanimously affirm SG dependence without raising this caveat.

Strong agreement on poly(A)-independent decay (C56-C61). Both evaluations support this paradigm-shifting finding. OpenEval notes poly(A) tail retention is a logical inference and that DCP2* has weaker expression, while peer reviewers universally accept the independence from canonical pathways as 'Surprising' and well-established.

Strong agreement on core mRNA shortening observation (C32-C39, C94). Both evaluations fully support the finding with converging evidence. OpenEval emphasizes statistical strength (p<10^-76 to 10^-307) and multiple controls, while peer reviewers describe data as 'convincing' and 'paradigm-shifting' without concerns.

Strong agreement on 5' directionality (C44-C50). OpenEval R1 includes these claims in its comprehensive assessment of shortening evidence. Peer R3 explicitly accepts '5' end RNA decay' with multiple validation approaches implicitly endorsed through positive assessment.

Strong agreement on XRN1 dependence (C51-C55, C96). Both evaluations support the knockdown findings. OpenEval notes incomplete knockdown as a limitation and the dramatic statistical change, while peer reviewers unanimously affirm XRN1 dependence without raising concerns about knockdown completeness.

Strong agreement on translation coupling (C69-C75, C79). Both evaluations support ISRIB findings. OpenEval identifies confounding issue that ISRIB inhibits SG formation, making interpretation ambiguous. Peer reviewers accept translation coupling without noting this confound.

Agreement on cycloheximide effects (C76-C78). Both evaluations support complementary evidence for translation coupling. OpenEval notes weaker effect than ISRIB and similar SG confounding issues. Peer reviewers group with ISRIB findings and accept translation coupling without distinguishing confounds.

Strong agreement on stress granule enrichment (C80-C82, C85, C104-C105). Both evaluations support the correlation. OpenEval emphasizes these are correlative observations from published data, not direct experimental evidence. Peer reviewers affirm enrichment without distinguishing correlation from causation.

Strong agreement on experimental design and quality control (C19-C21, C27-C31). Both evaluations support the setup. OpenEval details specific validation measures, while peer reviewers implicitly endorse through statements about 'convincing data' and proper methodology.

Strong agreement on technical approach (C22-C26, C93). Both evaluations praise the direct RNA-seq methodology. OpenEval describes it as appropriate experimental design, while peer reviewers explicitly highlight it as 'cutting-edge' and enabling the discoveries.

Agreement on mechanistic features (C66-C68). Both evaluations support correlative findings about CDS length and lack of ribosome association. OpenEval emphasizes correlative nature and speculative structural stability inference (C102-C103). Peer reviewers implicitly accept as part of overall convincing data.

Agreement on excluding 8-OxoG mechanism (C63-C65). Both evaluations support the negative result. OpenEval notes appropriate hypothesis testing and limited conclusion. Peer reviewers do not challenge these mechanistic findings, accepting them as part of the overall dataset.

Strong agreement on main conclusions (C3-C7). Both evaluations support the synthesized findings as paradigm-shifting. OpenEval notes conclusions are well-supported and appropriately qualified. Peer reviewers call findings 'novel, paradigm-shifting' and 'exciting,' accepting the proposed model.

Partial overlap on endonucleolytic cleavage (C62). OpenEval R4 addresses this as part of dominant-negative experiments, noting it's a reasonable but indirect inference. Peer R4 mentions XRN1 dependence but doesn't specifically address the endonucleolytic cleavage mechanism.

Partial overlap on ribosome quality control exclusion (C98). OpenEval R9 evaluates this as supported logical inference based on ISRIB/cycloheximide data, noting it's indirect. Peer R12 accepts overall model without specifically addressing this mechanistic exclusion.

Partial overlap on SG-P-body tethering hypothesis (C108). OpenEval R14 rates as uncertain, noting it's explicitly speculative with no direct evidence. Peer R12 accepts overall model as well-supported while recognizing mechanistic details remain incomplete.

OpenEval R15 evaluates background/context claims (C1-C2, C8-C18) as supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims, though they implicitly accept the study's motivation.

OpenEval R11 rates cross-cell-line P-body analysis (C83-C84) as uncertain due to significant limitations. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these negative results from published data analysis.

OpenEval R13 evaluates exclusion of protective SG hypothesis (C91) as supported through differential expression analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this alternative hypothesis testing.

OpenEval R17 identifies speculative claims and knowledge gaps (C99-C101, C110-C112) as uncertain, appropriately presented as discussion points. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these speculative elements.
